title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system that was escalated into an armed stop. The license plate reader misread a single letter and matched a BMW to a similar stolen vehicle, and the resulting alert was treated as grounds for enforcement. The failure sits at the handoff between the machine's output and the deputy's action, at the point where an unverified alert becomes the basis for drawing a weapon.

Catching it would have required independent verification of the alert before enforcement, which is what the vendor itself says should happen. A human check of the plate read against the vehicle in front of the deputy, or against the stolen vehicle record, would have surfaced the one-letter discrepancy. The system was used as though its matches were reliable on their own, and nothing in the deployment appears to have required that check.

What is not established is the cause. The sheriff's account that an illegal tinted plate cover produced the misread is the agency's assertion, not an independent finding, and the same agency's judgment that the deputy acted reasonably is likewise its own. No ruling or adjudication on either point is reported.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly held at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
